notes: Bulgarian is written in Cyrillic with 30 letters. Most of them stand for one sound each, and a word is said the way it is spelt, so once the letters are known almost any word can be read aloud.
Stress is not marked in normal writing and can fall on any syllable; learn it with each word (the 🔊 button, when your phone has a Bulgarian voice, or Ask Claude).
The letters look like Russian ones, but Bulgarian has no Ё, Ы or Э, and a few shared letters are said differently: Е, О, Щ, Ъ and Ь carry a note below.
Official Latin spellings (road signs, passports) write Ъ as "a" and Щ as "sht": Търговище is "Targovishte". This app writes Ъ as "ă" so it is not mixed up with А.
In handwriting and in italic print some small letters look different: т can look like m, д like g, и like u, and п like n.

letters.approx: An open "a", like the "a" in "father" but shorter.
Like English "b". At the end of a word it sounds like "p": хляб ends in a "p" sound.
Like English "v". It looks like a Latin B: that is the classic first trap.
Always the hard "g" of "go", never the "g" of "gem".
Like English "d" (the tongue a little further forward, touching the teeth).
A plain "e", like the "e" in "bed", also at the start of a word.
letters.russian: In Russian, Е at the start of a word or after a vowel sounds "ye". In Bulgarian it is always a plain "e": есен is "esen", not "yesen".

letters.approx: The sound in the middle of "measure" or "pleasure".
Like English "z". It looks like the number 3.
Like the "ee" in "see", but short. It looks like a mirrored Latin N.
A short "y" sound, as in "yes" or at the end of "boy". Mostly found after a vowel: чай, здравей.
Like English "k", with less breath after it.
Like English "l"; before е and и it is lighter.
Like English "m".
Like English "n". It looks like a Latin H: another early trap.
A short, rounded "o", like the "o" in British "pot".
letters.russian: Russian turns an unstressed О into an "a" sound. Bulgarian does not: an unstressed О stays an "o" (said quickly, it can move a little towards "u").

letters.approx: Like English "p", with less breath after it.
A tapped or rolled "r", as in Spanish "pero" or Scottish English. It looks like a Latin P.
Like English "s". It looks like a Latin C.
Like English "t", with the tongue touching the teeth.
Like the "oo" in "boot", but short. It looks like a Latin y.
Like English "f".
A breathy sound from the back of the mouth, like a soft "ch" in Scottish "loch". It looks like a Latin X.
The "ts" at the end of "cats", as one sound, also at the start of a word.
Like the "ch" in "chair".
Like the "sh" in "shop".
"sh" followed by "t", the middle of "ashtray". Ш with a little tail.
letters.russian: Russian Щ is a long, soft "shch" sound. Bulgarian Щ is simply "sht": нощ (night) is "nosht".

letters.approx: A short, relaxed vowel made in the middle of the mouth, like the "a" in "sofa" or the "u" in "hurt" without the r.
letters.russian: In Russian, Ъ is the silent "hard sign". In Bulgarian it is a real vowel, and a common one: България, къща, добър.

letters.approx: It has no sound of its own. It only ever comes before О, after a consonant, and the two together sound "yo": шофьор is "shofyor".
letters.russian: Russian uses Ь (the soft sign) in many places, often at the end of a word. Bulgarian uses it only before О and never at the end of a word.

letters.approx: "y" plus "oo", like the word "you".
"y" plus "a", like the start of "yard". It looks like a mirrored Latin R.
